newsitem.title: USA: New mutual funds tempt investors.
newsitem.headline: New mutual funds tempt investors.

text.p: Conventional wisdom among fund experts calls for sticking with mutual funds that have established track records of three, five or even 10 years. After all, how else can you judge how a fund is likely to perform?

Lately, though, some experts have been questioning that wisdom. In recent years, brand-new funds such as Dreyfus Aggressive Growth and Van Wagoner Emerging Growth have turned in sizzling profits for their original shareholders.
Meanwhile, veteran funds such as Magellan, which have been winners in the past, have suffered prolonged slumps or turned in mediocre results that could indicate fundamental problems.

In fact, new funds often have significant advantages over their older, more established siblings. For starters, new funds are relatively small, often running as little as $100 million in assets or even less. That means managers can put all of their money to work among the stocks that represent their best ideas.

By contrast, managers at more established funds whose long-term records have attracted many shareholders may have billions of dollars to put to work. For example, Magellan's asset base recently stood at more than $53 billion. Since a fund manager can buy only a modest fraction of any given company -- otherwise his purchases will drive the price up out of reach -- that pile of assets poses a problem: Where do you find enough good ideas to put all the money to work?

The choice for some big funds is to make very aggressive bets on big sectors -- for example, hot technology stocks. When those bets go wrong, the fund can stumble badly. Example: Magellan's big bet on bonds in early 1996. It caused the fund to trail the stock market by a significant margin.

An alternative approach is to spread a fund's assets among a huge number of different stocks. But that strategy forces the manager to buy stocks he or she may not have studied closely. It also creates a portfolio that more closely resembles the broad stock market indices; thus, it diminishes the fund's potential for superior returns.

New funds also get special treatment from their sponsors, who count on them to generate future profits. The fund companies generally make sure that their analysts' best ideas go to the new funds first; after the fund buys them, its brother and sister funds jump in as well -- driving the price of the stock higher.
In addition, fund companies often give their new funds more than their share of hot new initial public offerings. Such tidbits can make a big difference in the performance of a tiny fund.
Small funds also can afford to invest in the smallest companies. A fund like Magellan or Vanguard Windsor can't buy enough shares in a small firm to make a noticeable difference in its performance.
But new funds can buy shares of companies with tiny market capitalisations (share price times number of shares outstanding). Such stocks have generated the highest long-term returns on Wall Street.
That said, some new funds are mere marketing tools -- designed to lure investors into flashy and volatile market sectors that don't always live up to their promise.

Before you invest in a new fund, you should look for signs that it will be more than a flash in the pan. Ken Gregory and Craig Litman of the No-Load Fund Analyst in Orinda, Calif., argue that you should only consider investing in a fund under certain conditions.

Ideally, the manager should have a strong five-year investment record using an approach similar to that of the new fund. But that's relatively rare; thus, you might settle for a manager with a shorter record who is backed up by a strong research team at a well-respected fund company such as Janus or T. Rowe Price.

Among such funds, you might consider Janus Olympus (800-525-8983; $2,500 minimum; no-load), a new aggressive growth fund that recently held stocks in the technology and health-care sectors. Manager Scott Schoelzel established an impressive long-term record with a similar fund, Founders Growth.

Mark Yockey, manager of the Artisan International Fund (800-344-1770; $1,000 minimum; no-load), helped lead United International Growth Fund to strong returns before coming to Artisan. His recent holdings included stocks in Japan and Sweden.

Joseph Klein, who has eight years' experience as a health care analyst, manages T. Rowe Prices' new Health Sciences Fund (800-638-5660; $2,500 minimum; no-load). Recently, the fund held shares of small- to mid-sized biotechnolgy and medical device firms.

Finally, new funds often are launched to take advantage of a new growth sector in the financial markets -- such as emerging markets in the early '90s or computer-related technology a decade or so ago. Often, the new funds represent the only opportunities to invest in an exciting sector of the financial markets.

Example: T. Rowe Price Science & Technology, which opened in 1987, was one of the first no-load retail funds devoted to the technology sector. Investors who put $1,000 to work in the fund back then have $6,121 today -- a 22.3 percent average annual return.
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a freelance writer who covers financial issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
